name: NSFRIPPER (NES Music Extraction Studio)
tech_stack: Python (py65 6502 emulator, numpy, mido), REAPER JSFX, SQLite oracle DB, static site generator
card_summary: Reverse-engineers NES game music into MIDI and REAPER projects via 6502/NSF emulation, ROM-trace parsing against real hardware, and a custom JSFX synth. 321 games, 8,900+ MIDIs extracted, deployed as a browsable site. Includes a Bach-mashup side project. Active but stalled since April 2026 on an unmade listening decision.
page_summary:
NSFRIPPER builds a full NES-audio pipeline: NSF files run through 6502 CPU emulation (py65), capturing per-frame APU register state at 60Hz, which becomes 4-channel MIDI with CC11 (volume) and CC12 (duty-cycle) automation preserving the original driver's envelope, then REAPER .rpp projects using a custom unified JSFX synth called ReapNES Studio. For flagship games (Castlevania 1, Contra, Wizards & Warriors) it goes further, parsing the actual ROM sound-driver code and validating output frame-by-frame against Mesen-emulator hardware traces -- the project's fidelity hierarchy (Trace > SysEx > NSF emulation > CC automation > ADSR approximation) is a load-bearing rule repeated throughout its 40-rule architecture doc.

A SQLite-backed 'oracle' knowledge base (ANTIRIPPER/antiripper_v2.db) records extraction decisions, prevention patterns, and hardware facts as institutional memory across sessions -- a genuinely mature piece of infrastructure among Ted's projects. The site is live and generated deterministically from output/.

The last commit (2026-04-20) shipped a three-variant architecture specifically so Ted could ear-test and choose: Variant A 'Double Dose' (audio stems + JSFX), Variant B 'Live Wire' (pure JSFX/MIDI, playable live), and Variant C 'Ditto Head' (JSFX-rendered stems, deferred, never built). The README's own roadmap says the next step is simply: listen to A and B, decide whether to keep the Python stems pipeline, go JSFX-only, or build C. That decision was never made and never logged -- no commits since.

A Bach-mashup side project (bach_nes_mashup.py and siblings) pairs J.S. Bach MIDI with NES instrument timbre presets extracted from Castlevania/Contra/Metroid/Gradius stage palettes; see CHIPPEDONBACH.md for the full account, including two finished MP4 preview videos sitting at the C:\Dev root and 117 generated-but-unrendered projects.

Open technical items at last commit: whether the Python DSP fixes (14kHz analog lowpass, DC blocker, bandlimited pulse synthesis) need porting into the live JSFX synth too; a known ~15% non-linear-mix overload from summing independently-rendered stems in REAPER's bus; Metroid's intro track hangs the py65 emulator; a Capcom 6C80 ROM parser (~2 weeks estimated, not started) that would add ~40 games to trusted status; and three unsolved hardware mysteries called out explicitly in its own docs (why Castlevania produces noise drums without the $4015 bit-3 enable the spec requires; why SMB's driver writes a constant DC value to $4011 every frame; region-driver divergence between CV3's US and JP releases).

On disk, verified directly rather than taken from the project's own claims: `output/` holds 48 game folders and 2,063 MIDI files paired 1:1 with 2,063 RPP REAPER projects. The 40-rule figure in the architecture doc is also directly countable -- `.claude/rules/architecture.md` runs Rules 1-12, 17-18, 22 and 26-40 (topping out at "40. Noise HW Envelope Must Be Simulated in Capture"), with the remaining rules 13-16, 19-21 and 23-25 living in a companion `docs/ARCHITECTURE_REFERENCE.md`. The project's own driver-census claims are internally inconsistent in a small, honest way: CLAUDE.md cites both a "271-game census" (2026-04-14, and the 271 figure does sum exactly from the documented driver-family table) and a separate "298 games" register-level analysis three days later -- two different sweeps at two different dates, not a contradiction.

The three delivery variants behind the unmade ear-test decision have real architectural differences, not just naming: Variant A "Double Dose" plays 4-5 audio stems and 4 MIDI+JSFX tracks simultaneously by default, unmuted, and they are deliberately *not* sample-aligned (JSFX carries REAPER's MIDI-engine latency; the stems start exactly on bar 1), so the two can be A/B'd by muting one side at a time. Variant B "Live Wire" is pure JSFX -- 4-5 tracks running `ReapNES_APU2_v2.jsfx`, which resolves note data through a three-tier priority cascade (captured hardware SysEx replay, if present, beats CC11/12 automation, which beats plain keyboard ADSR). Variant C "Ditto Head" is, today, an unbuilt placeholder -- literally an identical copy of B's folder, standing in for a planned offline JSFX-to-WAV render pass that was never written. The project's own fidelity-gap table is candid about a real known shortfall: the audio stems carry five specific hardening rules (27, 30, 33, 34, 35) that the live JSFX synth only implements two of (27 and 34), with an explicit warning that JSFX "will sound SHARPER/BUZZIER than stems until Rule 35 ports" -- meaning the A/B ear-test Ted still needs to run isn't just a taste call, it's confirming whether that documented DSP gap is audible enough to matter.

The oracle database (`ANTIRIPPER/antiripper_v2.db`) is more structured than a simple lessons-log: seven tables (`hardware_facts`, locked and immutable; `prevention_patterns`; `driver_families`; `evidence_items`; `claims`, which agents may propose but never promote to accepted status themselves; `decision_records`; `attempts`), accessed only through a Python wrapper (`agent_oracle.py`) that enforces a preflight-attempt-outcome workflow rather than raw SQL access. Its own audit (2026-04-14) is honest about gaps: 105 of 225 "best output" games have no decision record (47%), the attempts and claims tables are empty, and 140 of 321 surveyed games remain unclassified entirely -- this is real infrastructure, used inconsistently, not a finished system.

The open wishlist (`state/wishes.json`, 20 items) contains two flagged critical and not-started alongside WISH16's Bach-render backlog: WISH01 would port CC11/CC12 automation handling into the flagship Console synth, which the project's own note says "fixes playback fidelity for all 1,099 projects at once" -- the single highest-leverage unstarted code fix in the family, distinct from the A/B/C listening decision, which is a choice rather than a fix. WISH18 flags that a large body of uncommitted Antigravity-session work (scripts, song sets, the Bach mashups, Castlevania 2/3 extractions, 36 documents, trace JSON files) sits unprotected, with its own text reading "One crash from gone." The project's `docs/ROM_MUSIC_MYSTERIES.md` documents at least two genuinely unresolved hardware puzzles beyond the noise-drum question already summarized: Super Mario Bros.'s extracted pulse periods measure almost exactly half (a ~2.003-2.005 ratio across 22 of 22 notes checked) of ground truth from Mesen traces, while the triangle channel is unaffected -- the current workaround transposes down 12 semitones without knowing why the discrepancy exists, suspected to trace to an uninitialized zero-page octave variable in the ROM's own driver code, and it remains untested whether this is SMB-specific or a wider pattern across the other traced games.
stuck_or_next: The A/B/C ear-test verdict is the single blocking decision -- listen to the two working variants, pick one, log it. Everything else in the pipeline works.

name: ReapNES Studio (ReapNESClod)
tech_stack: REAPER JSFX, C++/JUCE + CMake (VST3, Windows/MSVC), Python tooling, NES-MDB preset corpus
card_summary: REAPER-based NES 2A03 synth (JSFX + JUCE/VST3) with a 54K-preset corpus extracted from NES-MDB, project-generator scripts, and an analog console UI. Solved its core MIDI-keyboard-routing and DC-offset bugs, then was folded into NSFRIPPER on 2026-03-31 as the canonical synth source; no independent activity since.
page_summary:
ReapNES Studio set out to be a REAPER-based NES music production environment: pick a game's instrument palette, generate a ready-to-open REAPER project, play it live off a MIDI keyboard or import MIDI onto NES-timbre instruments. It shipped two parallel synth implementations -- a JSFX plugin and a JUCE-based VST3 (CMake, generated MSVC solution files, never fully wired up) -- plus a Python project generator and a 54,000+ instrument preset corpus extracted from the NES Music Database (reference/training data, not original work).

Its docs/BLOOPERS.md (14 documented blunders) and docs/SUCCESSANDFAIL.md chronicle a difficult early arc: JSFX plugins silently rejected as instruments over a missing in_pin:none declaration and a stray '//tags:' comment prefix; a Unicode character causing a silent compile failure; REAPER caching a broken compile until the file was renamed; '^' meaning POWER not XOR, breaking the LFSR noise feedback bit; and, most seriously, generated .rpp projects that could not get MIDI keyboard input routed to the JSFX instrument at all, because JSFX lacks the VST 'instrument' flag REAPER checks for live routing. A hand-built VST3-based project worked for keyboard input but couldn't be generated programmatically, because REAPER's RPP format for VST3 requires an opaque base64 plugin-state blob only REAPER itself can produce.

HANDOVER_KEYBOARD_AND_SYNTH.md documents the eventual fix strategy for the JSFX keyboard problem (diff a REAPER-saved working .rpp against a generated broken one; add a 'Keyboard Mode' toggle so the plugin ignores the MIDI channel filter for live input) plus explicit anti-patterns to avoid repeating. The final commit's message -- 'fix MIDI keyboard routing' -- indicates this was resolved before folding into NSFRIPPER, whose ReapNES_Console.jsfx inherits the working design.

NEXTPHASES.md describes an intended follow-on (Phase A: expose every NES timbre parameter as labeled knobs; Phase B: comparative timbre study; Phase C: educational website; Phase D: animated-knob YouTube pipeline; Phase E: drum tracker) with no commits recorded here -- any continuation happened inside NSFRIPPER instead, where the Bach-mashup and console synth work now live.

`docs/BLOOPERS.md` documents fourteen blunders, confirmed by direct count, each traceable to a specific root cause: a `//tags:instrument` line parsed as a comment rather than a directive (silently breaking MIDI routing); a missing `in_pin:none` declaration making REAPER treat the plugin as an effect rather than an instrument; a stray Unicode character causing a silent compile failure; REAPER's JSFX compile cache surviving even a deleted `reaper-jsfx.ini`, fixed only by renaming the file; guessed RPP tokens (`MASTER_SEND`, `REC_INPUT`) that REAPER silently ignored rather than rejected outright; a MIDI-input `REC` field that took four separate failed attempts at the right field count before the team reverse-engineered a REAPER-saved template instead of guessing further; a `SOURCE MIDIPOOL` and inline-event approach that both failed silently before `SOURCE MIDI FILE "path"` finally worked; an inaudible DC-offset mix (-0.784 silent, -0.45 while playing) that fooled the meters; `^` meaning power, not XOR, breaking the noise LFSR; every track initially playing all four APU oscillators simultaneously as an unintended wall of sound, fixed by adding a channel-mode slider; community-sourced MIDI files using inconsistent, effectively random channel numbers (one Mega Man 2 file had its "Air Man" part split across channels 1, 3 and 4), fixed with an auto-remap step; drum notes needing real decay envelopes rather than a bare on/off to avoid audible clicking; a 71-file classical-MIDI quality survey (rated Perfect/Good/OK/Bad, with only the top two tiers actually used) that turned up a "Für Elise" file whose piano part was, bizarrely, tagged as electric bass; and a hard practical limit of roughly three simultaneous voices for classical material, where Bach's two-voice inventions and the Goldberg Variations worked but full Beethoven symphonies did not.

The project's own closing self-assessment in `docs/SUCCESSANDFAIL.md` is unusually blunt for a status document: it states directly that "the user still cannot open a generated project and hear sound without manual intervention," against a scorecard of six documented successes and six documented failures -- an honest verdict, not a soft one, and part of why this project stayed archived rather than pushed toward a premature "done." The unresolved VST3/JUCE path has a named recommended fix that nobody executed: `SYNTHPROBLEM.md`'s "Option D" reads, in substance, that the user opens REAPER once, adds the VST3 manually to a track with default settings, and saves it as a template; the generator then extracts that exact block and reuses it (with modified parameters) for every future project, rated "low effort, one-time manual step, then fully automated forever" and marked as the document's own recommendation over three other options it considered and set aside (reverse-engineering the binary state blob directly, a ReaScript runtime swap between JSFX and VST3, or hunting for an undocumented REAPER preference to route keyboard MIDI into JSFX). `NEXTPHASES.md` lays out five dependent follow-on phases that were never started once the project folded into NSFRIPPER: Phase A (Synth Console Polish) would expose every hardware parameter as a labeled control; Phase B (Comparative Timbre Study) would mine the 54,000-preset corpus into structured per-game, per-channel envelope data; Phase C (an educational website extending the timbre data into per-game parameter pages) depends on B; Phase D (animated-knob playback visualization for YouTube) depends on A; and Phase E (a step-sequenced drum tracker, aimed at being more approachable than FamiTracker) depends on both A and B.
stuck_or_next: The VST3/JUCE path (working keyboard input, un-scriptable RPP generation) was never resolved. SYNTHPROBLEM.md's recommended fix -- save one project manually with the VST3 loaded, extract that block as a template -- was never executed. This is the best-scoped open technical problem in the whole family.

name: NESjamtools
tech_stack: Python (numpy/scipy render core), JSFX (live instrument), REAPER .rpp generation, MIDI
card_summary: A REAPER-based NES virtual instrument, not just an asset library: MIDI scores (or a live keyboard) become NES-accurate audio via a custom multitimbral JSFX synth plus a separate high-fidelity Python renderer. Ships 50 games as ready REAPER projects, hybrid stem+MIDI projects for 4 games. Sibling 'Instrument' layer to NSFRIPPER's 'Archive'.
page_summary:
NESjamtools is the instrument layer of a three-project family (Archive = NSFRIPPER, Instrument = this project, Score = shared MIDI). It doesn't try to be a byte-exact emulator; nesjam/nes_render.py is a hand-tuned NES-hardware-flavored renderer (non-linear DAC mix, bandlimited pulse synthesis, LFSR noise, triangle gate-hold, 4-pole analog lowpass and DC blocking) that turns a MIDI score into an accurate WAV bounce, while instruments/NESJam.jsfx is a single multitimbral REAPER plugin instance playing all four 2A03 voices live (channel 1->Pulse1, 2->Pulse2, 3->Triangle, 4->Noise).

build_all.py batches 50 representative NES games (Castlevania, Mega Man 2/3/4, Zelda, Metroid, SMB, Contra and more), sourcing from NSFRIPPER's output. Four games (Contra, Battletoads, Zelda, Wizards & Warriors) additionally ship as 'hybrid' projects -- accurate audio stems playing by default with muted, editable NESJam MIDI tracks underneath -- and as pure 4-track all-synth variants. A second install-free-VST path via the free 'Magical 8bit Plug 2' is documented as an alternative, including per-game ADSR translation tables.

HOWTO_LIVE_KEYBOARD.md walks through a dedicated _KEYBOARD_TEST REAPER project to isolate keyboard/synth problems from song-data problems. output.md (2026-06-11) is a detailed post-mortem mapping every specific complaint from an ear-test session (W&W noise sustaining after stop, Zelda pops on note edges, Double Dragon II sounding like noise from a mis-picked SFX-bank track, wrong track colors, a MIDI-device slot bug) to root causes and fixes -- all logged as Fixed except one, explicitly marked 'Awaiting your ears.' CLAUDE.md states the hard rule directly: don't claim 'sounds like the game' until the user ear-confirms in REAPER; the WAV renders are the verifiable artifact, the JSFX is unverified until loaded.

Assets on disk: 84 MIDI files, 23 four-track MIDI files, 50 NSF files, 50 game folders under projects/ and renders/. Git history is a single commit with no remote configured -- never pushed anywhere.

NESjamtools' own CLAUDE.md states the three-project "Archive / Instrument / Score" framing directly, in close to these words: Archive -- byte-exact register replay -- "NOT our job, that's NSFRIPPER"; Instrument -- a score or keyboard that sounds like the game -- "THIS is the goal"; Score -- editable MIDI, reused as-is from NSFRIPPER's own extraction work. That's a real division of labor stated by the project itself, not an outside inference. A small asset-count discrepancy is worth noting plainly: the `projects/` directory currently holds 54 subfolders, two of which are test scaffolds (`_KEYBOARD_TEST`, `_MAGICAL_TEST`), leaving 52 real game folders against the README's stated "50 games" -- a minor, unresolved gap between the documented and actual count. `renders/` holds 52 game directories and 71 WAV files total.

The ear-test postmortem (`output.md`) tracks four rounds of listening and fixes, game by game, and is worth citing specifically because it's the clearest evidence in this whole family of what "verify by ear" actually looks like in practice rather than as a slogan. Wizards & Warriors' noise channel sustaining after the note should have stopped traced to two separate bugs -- CC11 volume automation ignoring note-off events, and no handling for CC123 (all-notes-off) at all -- and was confirmed fixed by measuring the noise stem's RMS level drop from 0.826 to effectively 0.000000 after note-off, not just by ear. Zelda's popping on note edges traced to a missing DC blocker and was fixed the same way NSFRIPPER's own rules require (a proper high-pass filter, not a subtracted constant). Kid Icarus's over-long sustains were the same CC11 bug hitting a particularly "dense automator" driver; its FDS expansion-chip lead voice remains an acknowledged, documented, unrendered gap. Double Dragon II's reported "wall of noise" traced to a filename parser reading a literal "2" inside the game's title as a track index, which happened to select a sound-effects loop over the real song on a tiebreak -- fixing the parser also silently corrected the wrong track selection in seven other games (Super Mario Bros. 3, Zelda II, Castlevania II and III, Mega Man 2, Chip 'n Dale 2, and Ninja Gaiden II), a good example of one bug fix clearing several unrelated-looking symptoms at once. A reported "muffled reverby thud" on the Wizards & Warriors title-screen patch, played live from a keyboard, was run down with a small standalone Python port of the synth's DSP rendering a held middle C -- confirming correct pitch (262 Hz), a bright rather than muffled spectral centroid (6,907 Hz), a steady sustain, and no reverb anywhere in the signal path -- and was ultimately attributed to a REAPER monitoring/routing artifact on the tester's machine rather than a synthesis bug, a useful example of a complaint that DSP inspection cleared rather than confirmed. The one item still open at time of writing, "W&W Map: rhythm feels wrong," is explicitly marked "Awaiting your ears" rather than closed with a guessed fix -- consistent with the project's own stated rule (in its CLAUDE.md) not to claim a track "sounds like the game" until Ted confirms it directly in REAPER.
stuck_or_next: One open bug report ('W&W Map: rhythm feels wrong') is explicitly waiting on Ted's ear-test in REAPER; every other logged complaint is marked Fixed. Also has no git remote -- worth pushing once confirmed.

name: GlitchMario
tech_stack: Vanilla HTML/CSS/JS (site); Mesen 2, Python (mido, py65), REAPER + JSFX (pipeline it documents)
card_summary: A static documentary site narrating five days of trying to extract Super Mario Bros.' overworld theme from raw NES hardware registers, told as a timeline of 100 events, 17 'blunders,' and 30 NES-history milestones -- self-deprecating and specific, down to phase-inverting drums and a JSFX operator meaning exponentiation instead of XOR. Confirmed live and complete.
page_summary:
GlitchMario documents an NES-audio reverse-engineering effort as a narrative artifact rather than shipping a tool. The pipeline it describes: NES hardware APU -> Mesen 2 emulator trace capture (30,362 register changes across 21 parameters, 9,496 frames) -> mesen_to_midi.py (period-change detection, CC11/CC12 automation, producing 796 notes and 7,064 CC events) -> generate_project.py (a REAPER project with inline MIDI, 4 tracks) -> ReapNES_Console.jsfx (NES APU emulation inside REAPER: pulse, triangle, noise/LFSR, drum table) -> ear-verification, reaching '80% fidelity and climbing' by day five.

The site itself is a vanilla-JS single-page app: a 67.5KB data.json holds a project header plus an events array of 100 timeline entries (day/phase/title/summary/category/docs/terms), rendered by app.js into filterable timeline cards by category and by day, alongside a hardcoded 30-entry NES-history dataset (Famicom 1983 through GlitchMario 2026) and a 70+ term technical glossary.

Its greatest-hits blunder table is worth reading on its own: JSFX's '^' meaning exponentiation not XOR made the noise channel produce alien transmissions; a DC-offset formula that only worked at volume 15 caused drums to phase-invert mid-decay; a naive track-to-channel mapping turned Vampire Killer into a wall of sound; drums with no envelope sounded like popcorn; a synth ignoring CC11/CC12 silently replaced ground-truth envelopes with generic ADSR; a mixer formula error made pulse amplitude 15x too quiet while drums literally subtracted from the mix.

Git history: two commits, both dated 2026-04-01, remote at github.com/t3dy/GlitchMario. The live Pages URL was fetched directly and returns the expected page content -- a real, working, deployed artifact, not just a claim. The README is candid about scope: it documents research and failure, not a finished instrument. There is no ongoing 'next phase' implied anywhere in the file structure.

The site's own `data.json` (100 events) sorts every entry into one of seven categories -- architecture, blunder, discovery, glitch, milestone, narrative, rule -- which is what powers the timeline's category filter. Of the 17 blunders the project claims, 15 are individually identifiable as their own dated cards; the remaining two appear folded into adjacent narrative entries rather than standing alone, which is a minor structural quirk rather than a missing-content problem. Beyond the handful already well known from this cluster's other projects (the `^`-as-exponent noise bug, the volume-15-only DC-offset formula), the fuller list includes: a stray fourth Unicode/comment-parsing issue bundled into the same early blunder card as the `//tags:` and missing-pin mistakes; `SOURCE MIDIPOOL` items that render as visual-only stubs in the REAPER version used here, requiring `SOURCE MIDI` plus an explicit `FILE` reference instead; a gap in JSFX slider numbering that silently shifted parameter values on load; an early version of the project where every track played all four APU oscillators simultaneously before per-channel routing was added; a noise/drum channel that simply toggled on and off with no envelope until a 23-entry table mapping GM drum notes to period, mode, attack and decay values was built; a shipped Console synth that had no CC11/CC12 handlers at all, silently substituting generic ADSR envelopes for the ground-truth automation across all of its then-1,099 rendered projects; a minimal RPP header that loaded and played back fine but silently broke live keyboard input because it omitted several REAPER-required blocks (`ENVATTACH`, `SAMPLERATE`, `METRONOME`, `RECORD_CFG`, `MASTERPLAYSPEEDENV`, `TEMPOENVEX`, `PROJBAY`); and a `REC 0 0` (unarmed, no input selected) setting that later silently defaulted to the system microphone once a user armed the track.

The extraction numbers are more granular than the headline totals suggest: of the 30,362 captured register changes across 21 parameters, Pulse 1 contributes 353 notes, Pulse 2 341, Triangle 328 and Noise 168 in one internal count -- summing to 1,190, not the 796 figure quoted in the project's own README, a discrepancy this pass could not resolve and is flagging rather than silently picking one number. Other specifics: Pulse 1's driver caps its own volume at 12 rather than the hardware's full range of 15, and Pulse 2 caps at 11 -- a deliberate headroom choice in the original game's driver, not an extraction artifact. The triangle channel's linear counter takes 27 distinct values across 3,644 separate changes, meaning its "on/off" gating is considerably more nuanced than a simple gate. The noise channel uses seven distinct hardware period values, collapsed down to just four General MIDI drum categories in the final MIDI export -- the project's own docs call this lost distinction "the missing 30%" of noise-channel fidelity. The project's own closing fidelity scorecard rates itself unevenly by parameter rather than with one blanket number: pitch 98%, timing 94%, pulse volume 95%, pulse duty 100%, triangle gating 70%, noise envelope 30%, noise timbre 50%, with DPCM sample channel not applicable to this particular song -- a weighted overall of roughly 80%, matching the README's "80% fidelity and climbing" framing but showing plainly that the noise channel, not pitch or timing, is where the real remaining gap sits.

name: NESMusicStudio
card_summary: NSF/ROM -> MIDI -> REAPER/WAV/MP4 -> YouTube pipeline, possibly the actual current front-runner of the whole NES-music-tools cluster. Castlevania 1 complete (15/15 tracks, 0 pitch mismatches); Contra in progress (11/11 tracks, 96.6% volume match). Git-committed and actively worked, live site deployed.
page_summary:
NESMusicStudio shares NSFRIPPER's exact pipeline shape (NSF/ROM -> MIDI -> REAPER/WAV/MP4 -> YouTube) and may represent where that lineage actually continued under a different folder name after NSFRIPPER's last commit in April 2026 -- this needs a direct comparison pass before assuming NSFRIPPER itself is the most current state of the work. It is git-committed and shows genuine recent activity, unlike several of its siblings.

Confirmed progress: Castlevania 1 is complete with all 15 tracks extracted and validated against ground truth (0 pitch mismatches). Contra is in progress with all 11 tracks extracted and a 96.6% volume match against reference. The project deploys a live site at t3dy.github.io/ReapNES/.

A hardcoded path inside NSFRIPPER's own build_bach_preview.py (C:\Dev\NESMusicStudio\output\bach_mashups) references this exact folder name, confirming shared or overlapping lineage between the two projects -- worth resolving which one is now canonical before doing further extraction work in either.

`docs/GAME_MATRIX.md` gives real per-track fidelity numbers beyond the headline "complete"/"in progress" labels: Castlevania 1's 15 of 15 tracks measure 99.5% pulse-channel fidelity (zero pitch mismatches across 1,792 checked frames, with 9 pulse and 8 triangle "sounding" mismatches traced to fade-step edge cases and a one-frame linear-counter timing offset respectively) and 99.5% triangle fidelity. Contra's 11 of 11 tracks (validated against a 2,976-frame trace of the Jungle-theme) measure less evenly: 91% pulse-1 pitch match, 82% pulse-1 volume match, 70% triangle pitch match, and a notably higher 94% triangle volume match -- meaning Contra's remaining gap is concentrated specifically in triangle-channel pitch tracking, not a uniform shortfall across the whole extraction.

The project's own `docs/331UPDATE.md` (dated 2026-03-31) is explicit about lineage in a way that revises the open question `NSFRIPPER.md` raises: it states that "the NESMusicStudio (extraction pipeline) and ReapNES-Studio (synth/REAPER tooling) repos were brought together" -- a documented merge with ReapNES-Studio specifically, not with NSFRIPPER, and no document anywhere in this project claims NSFRIPPER lineage directly. As of that same update the project held 701 REAPER projects across 34 games, with 14 games added in that single session alone (Dragon Warrior, Final Fantasy, Metal Gear, both Ultima titles, Faxanadu, Gargoyle's Quest II, The Goonies II, Kid Icarus, Legendary Wings, Section Z, Silver Surfer, Strider, and Trojan) -- a considerably larger and more actively growing catalog than the two-game Castlevania/Contra headline suggests. Its docs also record specific per-game envelope "signatures" for five games' NES sound drivers, worth citing as evidence of real domain analysis rather than assumption: Super Mario Bros. uses a uniform five-step volume decay (64-56-48-40-32) with fixed seven-frame note lengths; Castlevania decays faster, in four steps (32-24-16-8); Mega Man 2 uses a minimal two-step decay (64-16) with one-frame arpeggios averaging 1.5 frames on Pulse 2; Metroid produces a distinctive "breathing" crescendo-decrescendo shape with long, averaging-38-frame notes; and Contra's driver produces a much larger attack transient, stepping through five volume values (127-51-42-34-25-17) at note onset.

The YouTube pipeline is a real, working ffmpeg invocation rather than a described intention: it pads a still screenshot to even pixel dimensions, encodes video with libx264 in still-image tuning mode at one frame per second, and encodes audio as AAC at 192kbps, falling back to a generated solid black frame via ffmpeg's `lavfi` color source when no screenshot is available for a given track -- the script also auto-generates a YouTube description file that names the specific sound driver identified for that game (for example, "Konami Pre-VRC, Maezawa variant" for one Castlevania-family title) alongside a timestamped track listing, mirroring the description-generation approach `build_bach_preview.py` uses for the Chipped On Bach previews.
stuck_or_next: Needs a direct comparison against NSFRIPPER to determine which project is the current canonical state of this pipeline before further extraction work proceeds in either.

name: REAPERBEYONDNES
card_summary: Declared successor extending NSFRIPPER's pipeline past the NES to GBA, SMS, Saturn, Genesis, SNES, GBC, and Virtual Boy. Heavily structured (per-chip project folders, its own agent-protocol document). Real, substantial work -- and not a git repository, a genuine loss risk.
page_summary:
REAPERBEYONDNES is a declared multi-system successor to the NES-only extraction work in NSFRIPPER and its siblings, scoped to cover GBA, SMS, Saturn, Genesis, SNES, GBC, and Virtual Boy sound chips as well. It is heavily structured for that scope: per-chip project folders, a tools/ directory, a kb/ knowledge base, and its own agent-protocol document ('THE_LITURGY.md') describing how sessions should work on it.

The most important fact about this project is not what it contains but what it lacks: it is confirmed to not be a git repository. Everything in it -- however much real extraction and tooling work has gone in -- currently exists in exactly one place, on one disk, with no version history and no remote backup. This is a materially different category of risk from every other 'stalled' project in this catalog, which at worst risks losing momentum, not losing the work itself.

The per-chip scope is concrete and directly verifiable by directory listing: ten system folders exist under `projects/` -- `gb_dmg`, `gba_directsound`, `gbc_sound`, `genesis_psg`, `genesis_ym2612`, `gg_sn76489_stereo`, `nes_apu`, `sms_sn76489`, `snes_sdsp`, and `vb_vsu` -- one fewer platform than the originally declared scope, since the project's own `memory/MEMORY.md` (dated 2026-04-23) explicitly records that Saturn support was deferred rather than dropped silently.

The honest, load-bearing finding from a direct inspection of those folders is that nothing is actually built yet in any of them: every single system's `renders/`, `tests/`, `jsfx/`, and `driver/` subdirectories contain only a placeholder `.gitkeep` file, with zero real code or audio present across all ten platforms without exception. What does exist is a first wave of research: a session referred to internally as "KB Wave 1" (2026-04-24) produced nine chip-reference documents under `kb/chips/*.md`, generated via parallel background research agents and confirmed to have all passed their own validation pass. The NES entry in that knowledge base (`kb/chips/nes_apu.md`) was not written from scratch -- it explicitly imports 19 of NSFRIPPER's 38 architecture rules directly, with the remaining 18 generalized out into project-wide protocol documents applicable across all ten target systems, which is a genuinely sensible reuse of NSFRIPPER's hard-won 2A03 knowledge rather than re-deriving NES facts a second time. A first vertical-slice implementation task, targeting the Sega Game Gear's SN76489 chip (`HANDOVER_03`), is marked "unblocked" and ready to start but had not been started as of this survey -- meaning the single most useful next action for this project is not more research but actually writing the first real chip driver against research that already exists and is sitting unused.

This changes the framing of the project's status somewhat from a pure inventory: REAPERBEYONDNES is not "heavily structured, substantial work already done and merely unprotected by git" so much as "heavily structured research and scaffolding, zero implementation, and additionally unprotected by git" -- both things can be true (the structure and the NSFRIPPER-rule reuse are real, careful work), but a reader should not infer from the elaborate per-chip folder layout that extraction code for GBA, SMS, Genesis or any other listed system actually exists yet. The `git init` and first-commit recommendation from `MUSICHACKING.md` remains correct and unchanged by this finding -- if anything it matters more, since a disk failure today would lose real prior-research documents (the nine KB chip references, the rule-reuse mapping) and not merely a head start, even though it would not lose working extraction code, because none currently exists.
stuck_or_next: git init and a first commit should happen before this project is touched further -- a five-minute, zero-downside action that removes a real data-loss risk.

name: nes-music-lab (NESMusicLab)
card_summary: Research-grade NES audio extraction and reconstruction work -- Castlevania analysis, trace conversion, MIDI export scripts. Has real, working code but is stalled and uncommitted to git.
page_summary:
nes-music-lab holds research-grade extraction and reconstruction code focused on Castlevania trace analysis and MIDI export, adjacent to but distinct from NSFRIPPER's own Castlevania work. It has a .gitignore in place but is not confirmed to have meaningful commit history, and is flagged as stalled -- real code exists, but it isn't clear whether it represents superseded early work later folded into NSFRIPPER, or a parallel line worth reconciling separately.

`CASTLEVANIAANALYSIS.md` documents a specific, real capture: a Mesen 2.1.1 Lua-scripted trace, 91.9 seconds long (roughly 5,524 NTSC frames), with the game's own music-engine tick rate measured at once every 7 frames (about 116.5 milliseconds, or roughly 8.6 Hz), and the song's full loop length measured at 256 engine ticks (1,792 frames, 29.8 seconds). Per channel within that loop: Pulse 1 carries the lead melody with 240 period changes and 18 distinct pitches spanning F2 to A4; Pulse 2 carries a countermelody with 289 period changes and the widest pitch range of the four channels, 23 distinct pitches from D3 to D5; the Triangle channel has 128 period changes across 9 pitches from A2 to C4; and the Noise channel fires roughly 469 hits per loop, all using a single hardware period index. The document also includes a full 79-note transcribed melody sequence and a period-to-note-to-cents-off lookup table, which is real, usable extraction data, not a placeholder or a stated intention.

The codebase backing this analysis is organized into a small formal package rather than loose scripts: `convert_trace.py` and `export_castlevania_midi.py` sit at the repository root, with a proper `src/nesml/` package underneath holding `dynamic_analysis/trace_ingest.py`, `dynamic_analysis/trace_convert.py`, `dynamic_analysis/state_trace_ingest.py`, and `export/midi_export.py` plus `export/reaper_export.py` -- alongside two top-level compatibility shims (`src/nesml/trace_convert.py` and `src/nesml/trace_ingest.py`) that duplicate the newer package-internal versions, a small piece of technical debt worth resolving whenever this project is next picked up. No document in either this project or NSFRIPPER's own files was found explicitly cross-referencing the other's Castlevania work, which means the relationship between the two remains genuinely unclear rather than settled one way or the other: this could be superseded early work later folded into NSFRIPPER's own Castlevania extraction, a parallel and non-overlapping analysis using a different evidentiary framework (the project's own docs describe a six-phase "evidence hierarchy and provenance" methodology, of which this Castlevania work represents Phase 1), or simply an independent research thread that never got reconciled with the sibling project. That ambiguity, not a lack of real content, is what actually keeps this project in "stalled, needs a decision" status rather than "safe to archive" or "safe to continue."

Neither project's docs mention the other by name in either direction, which is itself informative: if this were simply superseded early work later folded into NSFRIPPER, one would expect NSFRIPPER's own Castlevania documentation to credit or reference it, and it does not. The more likely reading, given the "evidence hierarchy and provenance" methodology this project's own docs describe as a planned six-phase framework (of which the Castlevania trace-and-transcription work above represents only Phase 1), is that nes-music-lab was conceived as a more rigorously evidenced, source-critical companion to NSFRIPPER's faster production pipeline -- prioritizing traceable provenance for each transcribed note over NSFRIPPER's broader per-game coverage -- rather than a competing or redundant effort. Whether that framing is accurate would require reading the later, unbuilt phases of its own methodology document, which describe intentions rather than completed work, so it remains an informed reading rather than a confirmed one.
stuck_or_next: Needs a comparison against NSFRIPPER's own Castlevania extraction to determine whether this is superseded, parallel, or complementary work, then either archive it explicitly or commit it and continue.

name: arpeggiator-composer
card_summary: A deterministic MIDI arpeggiator built specifically for REAPER, with a proper project structure (core/, jsfx/, reascript/, reaper_projects/, tests/). Not NES-specific -- a general composition tool. Stalled and uncommitted.
page_summary:
arpeggiator-composer is a REAPER-targeted deterministic MIDI arpeggiator, structured like a real small software project rather than a one-off script: a core/ logic layer, a jsfx/ folder for the REAPER-side plugin component, a reascript/ folder (REAPER's own Lua/Python API, run inside REAPER), reaper_projects/ for example projects, and a tests/ folder. Unlike the rest of this catalog it isn't NES-specific -- it's general-purpose composition tooling that happens to live in the same REAPER/JSFX ecosystem. It's flagged as stalled and uncommitted, so its actual completeness relative to its own test suite hasn't been independently verified in this survey.

The arpeggiator itself, per its own README, is a genuinely fully-specified feature set rather than a stub: six pattern shapes (up, down, up-down, down-up, as-played, and a seeded-random mode for reproducible randomness), tempo-synced note divisions from a whole note down to a 32nd, including triplets, a configurable one-to-four-octave range, step-skip patterning, a gate-length control from 10% to 200% of the available note duration, swing, legato with configurable overlap, one-to-four-voice harmony with independently configurable interval, spread and inversion settings, deterministic seeded velocity humanization (meaning the same seed reproduces the same "human" timing/velocity variation rather than being different every run), accent patterning, transposition up to two octaves in either direction, and a panic/all-notes-off control -- a feature list comparable in scope to a commercial arpeggiator plugin, not a toy script.

The project's folder structure matches that ambition: `core/` holds three design documents (`sequence_spec.md`, `state_model.md`, `transformation_rules.md`) rather than code, meaning the logic is specified but its actual implementation status relative to that spec was not independently verified in this pass; `jsfx/` holds five separate JSFX files (`arp_composer.jsfx`, `arpsynth.jsfx`, `simplearp.jsfx`, `theme_input.jsfx`, `voice_engine.jsfx`), suggesting the arpeggiator logic and a basic synth voice were built and iterated on as separate concerns; `reascript/lua/` holds three REAPER-API automation scripts (`create_test_midi_item.lua`, `insert_sequence_into_take.lua`, `sequence_debug_dump.lua`), with an empty parallel `reascript/python/` folder suggesting a Python REAPER-scripting path was planned but never started; `reaper_projects/` holds two example `.RPP` files; and `tests/` holds three specification documents describing test cases for note lifecycle, sequencing, and transformation logic, rather than an automated, runnable test suite. No document anywhere in the repository -- README, roadmap, engine notes, or a takeaways file -- states a reason for the project being stalled; the closest thing to a hard fact on this point is that the repository's own git history shows zero commits despite a `.git` folder existing, meaning the "stalled and uncommitted" status recorded elsewhere in this catalog is accurate, but genuinely undiagnosed -- nobody has gone back to ask why work stopped, which UNFINISHEDSTATUS.md already names as the one project in this family where that basic accounting has not been done.

Because the `.git` folder exists but holds no commits, the project sits in an unusual state relative to the rest of this catalog's "stalled and uncommitted" entries: REAPERBEYONDNES and nes-music-lab have no version control infrastructure configured at all, while arpeggiator-composer has the infrastructure in place and simply never used it -- a smaller, one-command fix (`git add -A && git commit`) than either of those two projects would need, and arguably an even lower-effort action item than the "run its own test suite" next step already identified, since the test suite is itself only specification documents rather than executable tests that could actually be run today. Until those specification documents (`test_note_lifecycle_cases.md`, `test_sequence_cases.md`, `test_transform_cases.md`) are turned into real, runnable tests, "run its own test suite" is not yet an available action -- the more honest immediate next step is writing the test harness the specs describe, then running it, rather than assuming a runnable suite already exists.
stuck_or_next: Run its own test suite (tests/) to establish real completeness, then decide whether to finish, archive, or fold useful pieces (e.g. its ReaScript patterns) into SYNTHBUILDER's own tooling.

name: FUGUEJUKEBOX
tech_stack: Python (scipy synthesis/effects, ffmpeg encoding); Next.js 14 / React 18 / TypeScript (browsing site, broken)
card_summary: Michael Maier's Atalanta Fugiens (1617) -- 50 alchemical three-voice fugues -- reimagined as 500 NES-square-wave chiptune variations (harmonic, scalar, and effects treatments). The music generation is genuinely complete and verified on disk; a companion Next.js browsing site was deployed to Vercel but is now confirmed dead (404).
page_summary:
FUGUEJUKEBOX transforms the 50 emblem fugues of Maier's Atalanta Fugiens into 500 chiptune MP3s: 50 emblems times 10 variations (3 harmonic elaborations, 3 scale-run/improvisation variants, 4 digital-effect treatments -- reverb, vibrato, echo, chorus), synthesized as square waves via a Python/scipy pipeline. Verified directly on disk: exactly 500 MP3s and 500 companion WAVs exist, matching the project's own completion reports -- this half of the project is genuinely done.

The website half is where it stalls. Two divergent folders exist: FUGUEJUKEBOX-website (the original working Next.js copy, linked to a Vercel project but never under its own git control) and FugueJukebox-repo (a separate git-tracked copy pushed to github.com/t3dy/FugueJukebox, whose own DEPLOYMENT.md explicitly excludes all 500 MP3s from the push due to GitHub file-size limits). The audio path baked into the React component is a filesystem-relative path that never resolves under real HTTP serving. The claimed live URL, https://fuguejukebox.vercel.app, was checked directly and returns HTTP 404 -- the site is dead, contrary to the README's 'LIVE ON THE WEB!' claim. A duplicate ~140MB copy of all 500 MP3s also sits in FUGUEJUKEBOX/music/emblems/, serving no purpose.

Per workspace hosting policy this project has no business on Vercel at all -- it's fully static.

The project's two website copies are confirmed genuinely divergent, not identical mirrors under different names: a direct file comparison between `FUGUEJUKEBOX-website/app/layout.tsx` and `FugueJukebox-repo/website/app/layout.tsx` shows real content differences, even though the two READMEs read as byte-identical text. The working copy's stack is a conventional 2024-era Next.js setup -- React 18.3.1, Next.js 14.2.0, TypeScript 5.3.3, the `lucide-react` icon library, custom CSS rather than Tailwind, EB Garamond for body text and Inter for UI chrome, a dark navy palette (`#0f172a` background, `#f1f5f9` text, `#d4af37` gold accent) -- a deliberately period-appropriate, alchemical-manuscript-adjacent visual design let down entirely by the audio-path and deployment problems described above, not by any lack of front-end effort.

The synthesis pipeline's actual algorithm is more specific than "harmonic elaboration" and "scale runs" as category labels suggest. `generate_variations.py` reads its 50-fugue source data directly from `C:/Dev/EmblemRoguelike/assets/fugues.json` -- a live cross-project file reference, not a local copy -- and builds three harmonic variants by adding fixed-interval voices beneath or around the melody: Variation 1 ("Root Position") adds a major third and perfect fifth below each note; Variation 2 ("First Inversion") adds a minor third below and a major sixth above; Variation 3 ("Close Voicing") adds a whole step below and a minor third above. The three scale-run variants only decorate notes longer than one beat, splitting each into three equal sub-durations and inserting two connecting notes: Variation 4 ("Diatonic") steps through a fixed C-major scale set, Variation 5 ("Chromatic") approaches chromatically from above, and Variation 6 ("Arpeggio") leaps by fourths. The four effects variants carry real, specific DSP parameters rather than generic labels: Cathedral Reverb runs at 70% wet with a 2.5-second decay and early reflections enabled; Vibrato Wobble combines a 0.15-depth, 5.5Hz vibrato with a 0.1-depth, 3.0Hz tremolo; Echo Cascade uses 60% wet feedback with triplet delay taps at 0.375, 0.75 and 1.125 seconds; and Spacious Chorus layers all of the above (50% reverb at 1.8-second decay, 20% delay at 0.5 seconds, plus the vibrato and tremolo settings) into one combined treatment. The actual synthesis engine, despite the README describing it as Web Audio, is pure offline NumPy and scipy: a square wave is generated as the sign of a sine function, a triangle wave from an arcsine transform of a sine function, both at a 44,100Hz sample rate with a linear ADSR envelope (release ramping to 0.01 rather than fully to zero) and headroom scaling of 0.6 -- there is no browser-side synthesis anywhere in the actual rendering path, only in how the README describes it.

Verified disk usage is larger than the README's own estimate: the 500 MP3s total roughly 144MB, close to the README's claimed figure, but the accompanying 500 uncompressed WAV intermediates add another 1.6GB, bringing the real `emblems/` folder to 1.8GB total -- and the duplicate copy in `music/emblems/` is a full duplicate of both the MP3s and WAVs, also roughly 1.8GB, not merely the ~140MB of MP3s alone that earlier documentation estimated.
stuck_or_next: Three-step fix: decide the canonical MP3 copy (delete the duplicate), get audio into a servable path (public/ folder or Git LFS), redeploy static to GitHub Pages instead of Vercel.

name: Emblems in 3D -- 8-bit Fugue Engine
tech_stack: Vanilla JS + Web Audio API, three.js 0.160
card_summary: Inside a three.js walkable reconstruction of Maier's Atalanta Fugiens, a hand-built NES-APU-style Web Audio synth plays all 50 of the book's three-voice canonic fugues as two pulse channels plus triangle bass, cycled through ten mined NES game-audio 'palettes.' Live in the world; jukebox/fugue browser pages are local-only by design.
page_summary:
EMBLEMSIN3D is a large three.js project turning Michael Maier's Atalanta Fugiens (1617, 51 emblems) into a walkable 3D world rendered in the book's own woodcut style. Its music slice, chiptune.js, is a small Web Audio engine loading pre-transcribed note data per emblem (from EmblemRoguelike's fugues.json: bpm, beats, and per-voice note arrays) and rendering it through an NES-APU emulation -- two pulse-wave channels via PeriodicWave at 50%/25% duty plus a triangle bass, each with per-note ADSR. This is transcribed playback in synthesized 8-bit voices, not generative composition -- the notes are Maier and Merian's actual counterpoint. gamesynths.js supplies ten 'game palettes' mined from 'nsfripper's CODEXSYNTH bench' (Mario, Zelda, Metroid, Castlevania, Contra, Final Fantasy, Kirby, Bubble Bobble, Bionic Commando, Wizards & Warriors), retuning duty cycle, ADSR, vibrato, and gain to evoke each game's voice; every fugue page cycles through all ten as it loops.

Three surfaces use this engine: the Fugue Jukebox (grid of 50 fugues), per-emblem fugue pages (10 cycling versions plus a scholarship accordion pulling Claudiens-DB commentary), and the Great Work cinematic tour (plays each emblem's actual fugue as the camera arrives). As of a later phase the same engine was vendored directly into the walkable world, so standing at a station plays that emblem's canon, off by default behind a mute toggle -- this part is confirmed live.

The standalone jukebox/fugue-page experience never got ported to the GitHub Pages build; it depends on absolute C:\Dev-rooted paths to sibling-project image assets that only resolve on a local dev server, and the project's own deploy-state notes flag this as intentional, not an oversight.

There is a real, small discrepancy in the source material worth stating precisely rather than glossing over: Maier's book itself is illustrated across 51 numbered emblem plates (EMBLEMSIN3D's own README describes "fifty-one emblems on one race course," and its gallery page independently counts "51 Atalanta Fugiens emblem plates"), while the music data specifically -- `fugues.json`, and every reference in `chiptune.js`'s own comments -- consistently says "50 three-voice canons." The most likely and simplest reconciliation, based on both figures being internally consistent within their own domains, is that one plate (conventionally the closing or epilogue-adjacent emblem) was never set as a fugue by Maier in the first place, meaning the correct framing is 51 emblems, 50 of which carry musical settings, rather than treating the two figures as contradictory.

`chiptune.js`'s actual synthesis is a real, Fourier-series-built approximation rather than a simple built-in oscillator type: both pulse channels are constructed via `createPeriodicWave` from a 32-harmonic Fourier square-wave series, with duty cycle as a genuine per-channel, per-palette parameter (not a fixed 50%/25% pair) -- the default palette uses 50% and 25% duty, but each of the ten game palettes sets its own values independently. The triangle channel uses the Web Audio API's native triangle oscillator type directly. Envelopes are linear attack-to-peak, linear decay to a sustain level, held, then an exponential release capped at 40% of the note's total duration; a second low-frequency oscillator modulates pitch detune in cents for vibrato, again with per-channel depth and rate. Voice allocation is pitch-aware: notes at or below MIDI note 52 preferentially claim the triangle channel first, then the two pulse channels, while higher notes reverse that priority -- a deliberate design choice putting bass content on the channel best suited to carry it. A permanently-active master bus applies a 4,400Hz low-pass filter plus a short, subtle delay-feedback loop (160-millisecond delay, 16% feedback, 10% wet) for ambience.

The ten confirmed game palettes carry genuinely distinct, specific parameters rather than cosmetic naming: Metroid uses the narrowest duty cycle of the set (12.5% on both pulse channels) with a pronounced 22-26 cent vibrato at 6.5Hz and the longest release of the ten, evoking its game's spacious, echoing soundtrack; Contra uses the hardest, fastest attack (2 milliseconds) matching its driving action-game pacing; Final Fantasy uses a slower attack (20-30 milliseconds) and the highest sustain level (75-80%) of any palette, closer to an orchestral pad than a percussive game-lead sound; and Wizards & Warriors uses the slowest vibrato rate (4.8Hz) and longest sustain and release of the set. Playback is triggered globally by a keyboard shortcut (pressing M, or a `&sound=1` URL parameter) over the walkable world rather than by proximity to any specific station, and the active game palette advances automatically by one step every time a fugue's loop repeats, not in response to player position -- meaning a player standing at one emblem long enough will hear it cycle through several of the ten palettes in sequence. A documented, non-obvious risk sits in the deployed Pages build specifically: its fugue data and synthesis engine are vendored, static copies checked into the deployment folder rather than live references to the EmblemRoguelike source project, so a future update to the canonical fugue transcriptions would not automatically propagate to the live site without someone remembering to manually re-copy the vendored files.
stuck_or_next: Local-only status for the standalone jukebox is by design (absolute-path dependency), not a bug to fix casually -- vendoring those assets for Pages would be real work. Folding ANTIGRAVFUGIENS's studio-effect variants into the main jukebox is the more natural next step and hasn't been started.

name: ANTIGRAVFUGIENS
card_summary: A small self-contained experiment reusing the same 50 Atalanta fugues and ten NES game-palettes, adding a second axis of ten weird studio effects per emblem plus six deliberately strange interactive audio toys. Not linked from the main site, not deployed -- the weirdest thing in the whole NES-music cluster.
page_summary:
ANTIGRAVFUGIENS is a four-file experiment branch (README, app.js, index.html, style.css) sitting inside EMBLEMSIN3D that takes the same 50 fugues and 10 NES game-palettes as the main jukebox and adds a second axis: ten 'studio tricks' per emblem, named for alchemical processes rather than ordinary studio-effect names -- tape delay, mercury vibrato, gated black-fire envelopes, albedo wash, rubedo phasing, ouroboric feedback, projection glitch, and more. Alongside these it offers six deliberately weird interactive toys: the Levitating Athanor, Ouroboric Dub, Dewpoint Runner, Sword/Egg Breakbeat, Rose-Garden Lockstep, and Sublimation Pinball. It only runs from the parent project's local server, isn't linked from the main site navigation, isn't listed in the deploy-state's published-paths, and has never been deployed anywhere.

The ten studio tricks are confirmed by name directly from the project's own README, though the file does not elaborate on each beyond its title: tape delay, mercury vibrato, gated black-fire envelopes, albedo wash, arpeggiated citrinitas harmony, rubedo phasing, ouroboric feedback, square-wave bass, volatile ladder tones, and projection glitch -- each one layered as a second effects axis on top of the same ten NES game palettes the main jukebox uses, meaning the experiment's full combinatorial space is ten fugues times ten palettes times ten effects, though nothing in the project suggests every combination was actually generated or is browsable as such; it reads as a toolkit for exploring that space live rather than a pre-rendered catalog of it.

The six interactive audio toys each carry a one-line mechanic description directly from the README, worth quoting rather than paraphrasing since they're evocative and specific: the Levitating Athanor works because "fugue pressure makes the plate hover; clicking vents heat"; Ouroboric Dub because "feedback draws a self-feeding circular serpent"; the Dewpoint Runner because "vibrato and delay turn the emblem into a moisture field"; the Sword/Egg Breakbeat because "short envelopes and downbeat hits cut the egg"; Rose-Garden Lockstep because "harmonies rotate geometric locks"; and Sublimation Pinball because "notes become charged pellets in a volatile cabinet." These read as genuinely playful, alchemically-literate interaction design -- each toy names a real operation or image from the Atalanta Fugiens/alchemical tradition (athanor furnaces, the ouroboros, sublimation, the philosophical egg) and maps it to an audio-reactive mechanic rather than treating the alchemical theming as pure decoration, which is exactly the standard the workspace's own governing rule for mechanics holds projects to: a player should be able to recover the symbolism from the behavior. Whether that standard is actually met in practice -- whether playing Sublimation Pinball genuinely communicates "sublimation" without being told -- would require actually running the toy rather than reading its one-line description, and was not independently verified in this pass; only four files exist in the whole project (`index.html`, `app.js`, `style.css`, `README.md`), so verifying it directly would be a small, bounded task if anyone wanted to confirm the standard is met before ever considering giving this experiment a real deployment.

Framed against the workspace's broader standard for how symbolic and mechanical design should relate -- a mechanic should let a player recover its meaning from how it behaves, without being told -- this experiment is a genuinely promising candidate to hold up against that bar precisely because its naming is so specific and so clearly drawn from the same alchemical vocabulary (athanor, ouroboros, sublimation, the philosophical egg, black/white/yellow/red stages implied by "albedo wash" and "rubedo phasing") that the source Atalanta Fugiens material itself uses throughout. That specificity is also exactly why it deserves more visibility than it currently has: a project this legible, sitting completely unlinked from any site navigation and undeployed anywhere, is a case where the gap between "built" and "seen by anyone but Ted running a local server" represents lost value rather than an unfinished creative idea still needing work.
stuck_or_next: Genuinely unintegrated -- would need to be folded into the main jukebox nav or given its own small deploy to be seen by anyone but Ted running a local server.

ANTIGRAVEMBLEMSIN3D is confirmed not a git repository -- a full mirror of EMBLEMSIN3D's static files (verbatim copies of chiptune.js, gamesynths.js, jukebox and fugue pages, unchanged) rebuilt around a Vite toolchain (node_modules, dist/, and generated/ folders are all present, so it has been run locally at least once). Its own README frames it explicitly as a mirror for experiments that should not disturb the original project. Two genuinely new prototypes live here, both unrelated to the fugue engine: antigrav.html (three.js 'antigravity' visual explorations -- levitating apparatus, furnace-accident cascades, and a stated-but-not-visibly-implemented idea about fugue/orbit synchronization) and gameforge.html (a game-design idea generator pulling from three SQLite databases -- Claudiens, ALCHEMYTIMELINEMAP, AlchemyBeatEmUp -- with no audio component at all). No live URL, no deployment.

The Vite setup is a real, working local toolchain rather than a stub: `npm install && npm run dev` opens the project at `http://127.0.0.1:5193/antigrav.html` and a second entry point at `/gameforge.html`, and the project's own `node_modules` confirms Vite, three.js, Rolldown and LightningCSS are all actually installed, alongside a separate Python `requirements.txt` for a style-seed generation step (`npm run styles:seed`) that produces visual variety for the antigravity scenes. `antigrav.html` itself is described in the project's own notes as drawing on "four styles... plus sampled megabase game-design themes": levitating emblem apparatus, furnace-accident cascades, a stated but explicitly unimplemented idea about synchronizing fugue playback to orbital motion, and planetary board-puzzle concepts -- the orbit-synchronization idea remains, per the project's own admission, notes rather than working code. `gameforge.html` is confirmed genuinely SQLite-backed rather than using static or mocked data: it reads directly from three real project databases -- `Claudiens/db/atalanta.db`, `ALCHEMYTIMELINEMAP/db/alchemy_timeline.db`, and `AlchemyBeatEmUp/db/alchemical_images.db` -- extracting emblems, dictionary terms, timeline processes, bestiary monsters, lab furniture, materials, failure modes and cascade chains via its own `npm run gameforge:data` build step, functioning as a genuine cross-project idea-generation tool rather than a superficial mockup.

Because this fork is a full pre-Phase-5 mirror of EMBLEMSIN3D rather than a minimal two-file sandbox, it also carries a considerable amount of additional, unrelated content beyond the two named prototypes: a 213-model relief gallery (`gallery.html`, spanning the 51 Atalanta plates plus 162 woodcuts from the separate Hypnerotomachia material), the camera-driven `grandtour.html` cinematic tour, an `experiments.html` page holding several small alchemically-themed minigames (Regulated Fire, Solve et Coagula, a dragon-tail-biting mechanic), a per-emblem 3D diorama generator (`scene.html`), and a fully realized bespoke three.js courtyard environment for Emblem VIII specifically, built with toon shading and a Sobel-filter ink outline effect and interactive athanor/furnace elements. None of this additional content is a music or audio project in its own right -- it rode along because the fork copied the entire EMBLEMSIN3D tree rather than cherry-picking specific files -- but it means anyone considering reviving this fork for its two named audio-adjacent experiments would also be inheriting a genuinely substantial amount of unrelated visual-design work, not a clean, isolated two-prototype sandbox.

The practical upshot for anyone considering reviving this fork is a genuine trade-off rather than a simple "worth it" or "not worth it" call: the two audio-adjacent prototypes (antigrav.html's visual explorations and gameforge.html's cross-database idea generator) are both real, working, and distinctive enough to be worth resurrecting on their own merits, particularly gameforge.html's live SQLite querying across three separate alchemy-themed databases, which is a more substantial piece of cross-project integration work than its brief README description suggests. But recovering either one means either extracting just those two HTML files and their JS dependencies into a smaller, purpose-built sandbox, or accepting the full weight of the inherited EMBLEMSIN3D mirror (the 213-model gallery, the cinematic tour, the Emblem VIII courtyard, and the several unrelated minigames) that currently surrounds them. No document in the project states a preference between those two paths, so it remains an open decision rather than a next step already scoped.
stuck_or_next: The 'fugue/orbit synchronization' idea mentioned in antigrav.html's own notes was never actually implemented -- the only concrete unfinished thread here, if anyone wants to resurrect this fork.

name: Chipped On Bach
tech_stack: Python (numpy, mido), REAPER JSFX (ReapNES synth family), ffmpeg
card_summary: J.S. Bach MIDI (Goldberg Variations, Well-Tempered Clavier, Two-Part Inventions, Cello Suite No. 1) paired with NES instrument timbre presets extracted from Castlevania, Contra, Metroid, and Gradius stage palettes, rendered through NSFRIPPER's own synth pipeline. Two finished preview videos exist; ~117 generated projects mostly never rendered to WAV.
page_summary:
Chipped On Bach is not a separate synthesis engine -- it's NSFRIPPER's own extraction/synth pipeline pointed at classical MIDI instead of extracted game MIDI. bach_nes_mashup.py, bach_render_mashup.py, and build_bach_preview.py pair Bach MIDI files with NES instrument presets mined from real game soundtracks, each stage contributing a distinct pulse-duty-cycle character, and render the combination through the same ReapNES JSFX synth family used everywhere else in the project.

Two finished video artifacts sit at the C:\Dev root: Chipped_On_Bach_Preview.mp4 (70.6MB, 39 tracks, 1:12:36 total) and Chipped_on_Bach_Preview_less_glitchy.mp4 (39MB, a curated 4-track, 7:28 re-cut). Both carry .txt sidecars drafted as YouTube descriptions, confirming synthesis runs through the real NES Audio Processing Unit emulation via ReapNES JSFX, not a mockup. A BACH_MAP dictionary in the preview builder expands short filenames to full catalog titles with BWV numbers, ready to reuse if these are ever actually published.

NSFRIPPER's own wishlist (state/wishes.json, item WISH16) flags that roughly 117 Bach-fugue by game-palette REAPER projects were generated but most were never rendered to WAV, likely interrupted by a crash -- still open, marked low priority. This is genuinely low-effort follow-on work: the expensive generation step already ran; only the render pass is incomplete.

A path worth checking before reusing these scripts: build_bach_preview.py reads source WAVs from C:\Dev\NESMusicStudio\output\bach_mashups, the pre-rename project path -- and NESMusicStudio now also exists as a separate, currently active folder, so this hardcoded path should be re-verified rather than trusted blindly.

The pairing algorithm is meaningfully more sophisticated than a fixed 1:1 mapping between a Bach piece and a game palette: `bach_nes_mashup.py` (1,029 lines) builds the full cross-product of every available Bach (and, per the script's own scope, some Mozart and Beethoven) piece against every NES stage preset, then scores each resulting pair using a hardcoded mood-compatibility matrix keyed on descriptive tags -- a "dark" piece paired with an "eerie" stage scores highly (9 out of a stated scale), a "bright" piece against an "aggressive" stage scores lower (5) -- and a `--render-best` mode greedily selects the top-scoring pairs while capping repetition (no more than two renders per Bach piece, no more than three per NES stage), so the eventual track list is a curated, mood-matched selection rather than an arbitrary or exhaustive one. Instrument routing within each render is also automatic rather than manually assigned: MIDI channels are sorted by average pitch and note density into triangle (bass), pulse 1 (the busiest or lead line), pulse 2, and noise (reserved for MIDI channel 9, the conventional drum channel), inferred fresh from each source file rather than hand-mapped per piece.

A genuine discrepancy surfaced in a closer read of the actual preset data, worth flagging rather than smoothing over: `bach_nes_mashup.py`'s own `STAGE_PRESETS` table -- the actual source of the timbre palettes used in generation -- contains zero Metroid entries at all; the games actually represented are Castlevania (5 stage presets), Contra (4), Journey to Silius (5), Gradius (3), Ghosts 'n Goblins (1), and Bionic Commando (6), 24 presets in total. Yet both finished preview MP4s' track listings include pieces explicitly labeled "x Metroid," and the separate preview-description builder script carries a bare `Metroid` entry with no associated stage detail -- meaning the Metroid material heard in the finished previews was very likely generated through a different code path or preset source than the one this pass located, not fabricated, but not traceable to the specific script examined here either.

The BACH_MAP dictionary that expands short internal filenames into full catalog titles for YouTube descriptions is a real, populated table (roughly 35 entries), not a placeholder -- confirmed examples include `Fugue2` expanding to "Well-Tempered Clavier, Fugue No. 2 in C minor, BWV 847," `invent1` to "Two-Part Invention No. 1 in C major, BWV 772," `var3c1` to "Goldberg Variations, Variation 3 (Canon at the Unison), BWV 988," and `pre1` to "Cello Suite No. 1, Prelude in G major, BWV 1007." WISH16's recorded status in NSFRIPPER's own wishlist is, precisely, "blocked" rather than simply "open" -- its exact recorded description reads "Render WAVs for the 117 Bach fugue mashup REAPER projects," with the rationale "Fugues 1, 2, 5, 7 crossed with every CV1 and Contra palette exist as RPPs but have zero WAV files; likely interrupted by crash." The two finished preview artifacts have precise, confirmed sizes and durations: `Chipped_On_Bach_Preview.mp4` is 70,594,367 bytes (about 67.3 MiB) and runs 1 hour, 12 minutes and 36 seconds across 39 tracks, opening with "Goldberg Variations, BWV 988 x Metroid" and carrying several informal editorial notes in its own track list such as "[good harmonies noisy pulse]" and "[filthiest lead]"; the curated re-cut, `Chipped_on_Bach_Preview_less_glitchy.mp4`, is 39,003,653 bytes (about 37.2 MiB) and runs 7 minutes and 28 seconds across exactly 4 tracks. Both sidecar text files end with an identical sentence confirming genuine hardware-accurate synthesis rather than a mockup: "All synthesis uses the NES Audio Processing Unit (2A03) via ReapNES JSFX."
stuck_or_next: Re-run the render pass on the ~117 generated-but-unrendered Bach x game-palette projects. Verify the NESMusicStudio path is still correct before doing so.

name: Bach Studies (scholarship, not music)
tech_stack: SQLite, Python (PyMuPDF), vanilla static HTML, GitHub Actions (unused)
card_summary: A DH-framework scaffold for Bach scholarship (SQLite to Python to static HTML), not Bach music-making. 13 books converted to a corpus, a mostly-empty auto-generated 13,815-page 'dictionary' behind only 12 real entries. Never pushed to a git remote. Zero audio, MIDI, or synthesis code anywhere -- easy to confuse with Chipped On Bach by name alone.
page_summary:
BachStudies follows the same DH-framework pattern as several of Ted's scholarly portals: a corpus/ of 13 Bach-scholarship books (Wolff, Stauffer, Leaver, Demeyere's Art of Fugue, Rathey, Forkel, and others) converted from PDF to Markdown, feeding a SQLite database and a static-HTML build. Its CLAUDE.md states clean system invariants (data flows one direction, source to DB to HTML; the DB is the only source of truth) and its own roadmap marks several phases 'READY,' but on inspection those phases ran only shallowly.

The database currently holds 12 primary entities, 12 scholars, 12 bibliography entries, 12 dictionary terms (Fugue, Cantata, Chorale, Counterpoint, Basso continuo, Passion, Thomaskirche, Leipzig, Cothen, Weimar, Bach Revival, Baroque -- all genuinely reviewed and high-confidence), and zero essays. But the committed site/dictionary/ folder contains 13,815 HTML pages, of which all but those 12 are essentially empty stubs left over from an indiscriminate corpus-extraction pass whose output no longer matches the reseeded 12-row database -- a stale, unpruned build sitting in git.

BACHPEDAGOGY.md proposes an ambitious four-tier music-theory curriculum with short public-domain-MIDI audio snippets as illustrative clips -- the only place audio is mentioned anywhere in this project -- but it is entirely unbuilt: no theory_lessons table, no MIDI rendering code, nothing beyond the planning document. The repo has no git remote configured at all, so its GitHub Actions Pages-deploy workflow, though well-formed, has never actually run.

This is a text and research project with no music-composition or audio-production component. It should not be filed alongside the actual music-hacking projects in this catalog, despite sharing Bach's name with Chipped On Bach.

The project's own `docs/ROADMAP.md` marks its eight phases with real, differentiated statuses rather than a uniform "in progress": Phase 0 (Source Conversion), Phase 1 (Database Scaffold), Phase 2 (Corpus Extraction), Phase 4 (Site Generation), Phase 5 (Validation), and Phase 6 (Deployment) are all marked READY, while Phase 3 (AI Enrichment) and Phase 7 (Content Review) are marked PLANNED rather than started -- meaning the honest gap is specifically in the two phases that would have turned raw extracted text into reviewed, trustworthy essay content, exactly the gap that produced the 13,815 largely-empty dictionary stub pages described above.

The 13-book corpus is a real, confirmed list rather than a round number: it includes Demeyere's Art of Fugue (also separately cataloged in this library), Stauffer's Organ Preludes (also separately cataloged), Rathey's Bach's Major Vocal Works, Christoph Wolff's Johann Sebastian Bach: The Learned Musician (Norton, 2000), Leaver's edited Routledge Research Companion to J.S. Bach (also separately cataloged), Forkel's foundational early biography J.S. Bach: His Life, Art, and Work, Loewe's St John Passion theological commentary (also separately cataloged), the Pincus guitar-tablature volume (also separately cataloged), a Peters/Sanders collection of contextual Bach studies, a Delphi Masterworks edition and a second Delphi Great Composers volume on Bach, a beginner-oriented Dutkanicz volume titled My First Book of Bach, and a standalone Dover edition pairing the Art of the Fugue with the Musical Offering -- meaning four of the thirteen books feeding this text-only scholarship project are the exact same physical books already cataloged separately, with their own page_summary entries, in this music-technology library, a genuine and useful cross-reference between the two catalogs rather than a coincidence. `BACHPEDAGOGY.md`'s proposed four-tier curriculum is fully specified rather than a vague sketch: Tier 1 "Gateway" assumes no prior music knowledge and covers ten foundational topics (fugue, counterpoint, chorale, key, aria, canon, passion, oratorio, basso continuo, prelude); Tier 2 "Explorer" assumes basic music literacy and covers ten more topics including subject/answer relationships, invertible counterpoint, da capo and ritornello form, chorale harmonization, and text-painting; Tier 3 "Student" assumes the reader can already analyze chord progressions and covers ten topics including stretto, augmentation and diminution, permutation fugue, musical rhetoric, the Neapolitan sixth, and the galant-style controversy; and Tier 4 "Scholar" is explicitly graduate-level and research-oriented, covering eight topics including computational fugue analysis, Kirkendale's Quintilian-rhetoric hypothesis about fugal structure, the Rifkin one-voice-per-part performance-practice debate, source criticism and dating methods, and the stile antico tradition -- each tier's topic list cites a specific source within the 13-book corpus (for example, a given topic citing "Demeyere Ch. 1" or "Rathey Appendix B"), and the document's own appendix independently confirms the corpus size, stating its topics were "extracted from 13 corpus files (11M of scholarly text)." None of this curriculum has been built into working code -- no lesson-content database table, no audio-snippet rendering pipeline -- and it remains, honestly, a well-specified plan rather than a feature.
stuck_or_next: Prune the ~13,793 junk dictionary stub pages before the site is presentable; the underlying scholarship (12 solid entries) is fine as far as it goes but the roadmap's Phase 3 (AI enrichment) and Phase 7 (human review) were never started.
